vulnerabilities.explanation: isGranted computes _currentBalance = token.balanceOf(_who) + lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who) and compares against plugin.minProposerVotingPower(). Because balanceOf reflects transient ERC20 balances, any token supporting flash loans or flash mints allows temporary satisfaction of the threshold without locking tokens.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Flash-loan N tokens where N >= minProposerVotingPower. 2. Call createProposal; isGranted returns true via balanceOf. 3. Lock tokens, vote, and auto-execute via EarlyExecution. 4. Unlock and repay flash loan. No locked balance is required at proposal creation.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Replace the check with only lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who) >= minProposerVotingPower. Store proposal creator and required lock amount in the proposal struct; prevent unlocking until proposal lifecycle ends.

ground_truth.description: The MinVotingPowerCondition contract allows any users who hold at least plugin.minProposerVotingPower() amount of tokens (locked in the LockManager or in their token balance) to create a proposal and execute LockToVote.createProposal. This logic can be easily bypassed if the token allows flashloan or flashmint. Given that isGranted checks the user's token balance (line 45: token.balanceOf(_who) + lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who)), the user does not even need to lock the flashloaned amount into the LockManager to be able to create and spam proposals.

This logic can be easily bypassed if the token allows flashloan or flashmint. Given that isGranted checks the user's token balance (line 45: token.balanceOf(_who) + lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who)), the user does not even need to lock the flashloaned amount into the LockManager to be able to create and spam proposals.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. Flashloan the token.
2. Create the proposal (isGranted passes because token.balanceOf includes flashloaned amount).
3. Lock + vote the proposal and auto-execute it (EarlyExecution).
4. Unlock the tokens.
5. Repay the flashloan.
All in the very same transaction.
ground_truth.fix_description: Avoid using the token's balance and require the user to only use the locked amount. Change line 45 from 'token.balanceOf(_who) + lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who)' to just 'lockManager.getLockedBalance(_who)'. Store the proposal's creator in the proposal struct and require that the locked amount required to create the proposal won't be unlockable until the proposal ends.

vulnerabilities.explanation: totalControlled() calls oracle.latestRecord() and uses record.currentTotalValidatorBalance / cumulativeProcessedDepositAmount with no timestamp freshness check. ethToMETH() and mETHToETH() (called by stake() and _unstakeRequest()) rely on this value to compute mint/burn amounts.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Oracle record becomes stale after slashing (overstates totalControlled) or rewards (understates). 2. Attacker calls stake() with ETH when totalControlled is understated -> receives excess mETH. 3. Or calls unstakeRequest() when overstated -> receives excess ETH. 4. Profit extracted from protocol or other users once oracle updates.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: In totalControlled(), require block.timestamp - record.timestamp <= MAX_ORACLE_DELAY (e.g. 1 hour) and revert otherwise; enforce check before any mint/burn path.

ground_truth.description: Staking.totalControlled() derives the mETH/ETH exchange rate inputs from oracle.latestRecord() without validating the record timestamp. If the oracle lags significant state changes (e.g., validator rewards or slashing), the resulting rate becomes stale. An attacker can exploit this by timing mint/burn operations against outdated totals: redeeming mETH for excess ETH when a slashing is not yet reflected (overstated totalControlled()), or depositing ETH to mint excess mETH when recent rewards are not yet reflected (understated totalControlled()), extracting value from other users.
ground_truth.root_cause: Staking.totalControlled() derives the mETH/ETH exchange rate inputs from oracle.latestRecord() without validating the record timestamp. If the oracle lags significant state changes (e.g., validator rewards or slashing), the resulting rate becomes stale. An attacker can exploit this by timing mint/burn operations against outdated totals: redeeming mETH for excess ETH when a slashing is not yet reflected (overstated totalControlled()), or depositing ETH to mint excess mETH when recent rewards are not yet reflected (understated totalControlled()), extracting value from other users.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
Slashing scenario:
1. Validators are slashed, reducing the actual ETH controlled by the protocol
2. Oracle has not yet updated to reflect the slashing
3. totalControlled() returns the old (higher) value
4. Attacker calls unstakeRequest() and receives more ETH per mETH than they should
5. Other users bear the loss when the oracle updates

Reward scenario:
1. Validators earn significant rewards
2. Oracle has not yet updated to reflect the new rewards
3. totalControlled() returns the old (lower) value
4. Attacker calls stake() and receives more mETH per ETH than they should
5. The mETH is worth more once the oracle updates
ground_truth.fix_description: Enforce freshness validation for oracle records when minting or burning mETH. The Oracle.latestRecord() function has no sanity checks - it simply returns _records[_records.length - 1]. The validations should be implemented on the caller side, specifically in the Staking.totalControlled() function.

vulnerabilities.explanation: unstakeRequest calls mETHToETH to fix ethAmount at request time using current totalControlled(). This rate is stored in UnstakeRequest and used at claim. Subsequent slashing (via oracle cumulativeDrawdown) or rewards are not applied to pending requests, breaking socialization. Pending mETH remains in circulation (transferred to UnstakeRequestsManager but not burned), continuing to dilute rewards via totalSupply() in mETHToETH/ethToMETH.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: User A and B both call _unstakeRequest(1000 mETH) when rate=1.0, locking 1000 mETH each. Oracle then reports slashing reducing totalControlled by 10%. User A frontruns claim and receives full ETH; User B's claim reverts due to insufficient allocated ETH. Alternatively, pending requests accrue rewards they should not receive.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Burn mETH at request time or snapshot totalControlled per request; settle claims using latest oracle/liquidity state at claim to socialize losses; exclude locked mETH from reward calculations.

ground_truth.description: When Staking.unstakeRequest() is called, the mETH/ETH rate is fixed and does not reflect slashing or rewards that may occur by the time Staking.claimUnstakeRequest() is executed. If two users create requests concurrently and losses arrive afterward, those losses are not socialized across them. One request may be fully paid while the other may revert on claim due to insufficient allocated funds. This can be exacerbated by frontrunning updates to LiquidityBuffer.cumulativeDrawdown(), enabling informed actors to anticipate loss application. Rewards are also misallocated: requests lock mETH but do not burn it until UnstakeRequestsManager.claim(), so these shares continue participating in reward distribution, diluting rewards for users who have not requested to unstake.

If two users create requests concurrently and losses arrive afterward, those losses are not socialized across them. One request may be fully paid while the other may revert on claim due to insufficient allocated funds. This can be exacerbated by frontrunning updates to LiquidityBuffer.cumulativeDrawdown(), enabling informed actors to anticipate loss application. Rewards are also misallocated: requests lock mETH but do not burn it until UnstakeRequestsManager.claim(), so these shares continue participating in reward distribution, diluting rewards for users who have not requested to unstake.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
Loss scenario:
1. Alice and Bob each hold 100 mETH, pool controls 200 ETH
2. Alice calls unstakeRequest(100 mETH), rate fixed at 1:1, expects 100 ETH
3. Bob calls unstakeRequest(100 mETH), rate fixed at 1:1, expects 100 ETH
4. Slashing event occurs, pool now only has 150 ETH
5. Protocol allocates 100 ETH to Alice's claim (succeeds)
6. Bob's claim reverts due to insufficient funds (only 50 ETH left)
7. The slashing loss was not socialized - Alice escaped, Bob bears full loss

Reward dilution scenario:
1. Alice and Bob each hold 100 mETH, pool controls 200 ETH
2. Alice calls unstakeRequest(100 mETH) - shares locked but not burned
3. 100 ETH reward is distributed across 200 mETH (all shares still exist)
4. Only ~50 ETH is attributed to Bob instead of ~100 ETH
5. Alice's locked shares continue to earn rewards until she claims
ground_truth.fix_description: Align withdrawal settlement with the latest protocol state to socialize slashing and adjust reward accounting so pending unstakes do not accrue or dilute rewards. The client acknowledged this as a protocol design trade-off.

vulnerabilities.explanation: validateUserOp performs an external self-call via `this.isValidSignature(...)`. This sets msg.sender to the wallet address inside BaseAuth.signatureValidation and BaseAuth.isValidSignature. Static signatures (flag 0x80) are validated against the expected caller (entrypoint) in signatureValidation: `if (addr != address(0) && addr != msg.sender) revert InvalidStaticSignatureWrongCaller`. The mismatch causes revert for any static signature bound to the entrypoint.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Wallet owner sets a static signature bound to the entrypoint address via setStaticSignature. 2. User submits a UserOperation through the EntryPoint. 3. validateUserOp executes the external isValidSignature call. 4. signatureValidation sees msg.sender == wallet (not entrypoint) and reverts. 5. UserOperation validation fails, causing permanent DoS for operations relying on that static signature.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Replace the external self-call with an internal call (e.g., directly invoke the signature validation logic or use a view function that preserves the original caller context) and propagate the intended caller (entrypoint) into the validation.

Call LockManager.vote() (which calls plugin.vote()) casting YES to trigger _attemptEarlyExecution and execute proposal. 4. Call LockManager.unlock() to release tokens. 5. Repay flashloan. 1. Flashloan the needed amount.
2. Lock the flashloaned amount via LockManager.lock().
3. Cast a 'YES' vote via LockManager.vote() which triggers LockToVotePlugin._attemptEarlyExecution().
4. Proposal executes immediately in same transaction.

vulnerabilities.explanation: The signed quote digest is computed via keccak256(abi.encode(sender, key, params.zeroForOne, maxAmountIn, maxExchangeRate, exchangeRateDenom, nonce, expiryTime)) with no EIP-712 domain separator containing chainId or contract address. CREATE3 deployment allows identical PoolKey on multiple chains.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Obtain valid signature+nonce for a quote on chain A. 2. Deploy identical hook+pool via same CREATE3 salt on chain B. 3. Submit identical hookData (same nonce, expiry, signature) to beforeSwap on chain B. 4. SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow succeeds and swap executes.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Include an EIP-712 domain separator with chainId and verifying contract address in the digest computation.

ground_truth.description: Both UniswapV4KEMHook and PancakeSwapInfinityKEMHook rebuild a quote digest by hashing sender, key, params.zeroForOne, maxAmountIn, maxExchangeRate, exchangeRateDenom, nonce, and expiryTime. The tuple ties the authorization to the router (sender), the full PoolKey (which includes the hook address), trade direction, price and input caps, nonce and expiry. Crucially, no domain separator is folded in: chain ID, deployment salt, and contract identity outside key are absent. If the same hook instance (or the same PoolKey) is deployed on multiple networks, as CREATE3-based salt mining allows, an attacker can lift any valid signature+nonce from chain A and replay it on chain B. Because the digest matches, SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow succeeds and the swap executes without the signer's intention. That breaks the core guarantee that signed quotes are single-instance authorizations, allowing cross-chain replay swaps.

The tuple ties the authorization to the router (sender), the full PoolKey (which includes the hook address), trade direction, price and input caps, nonce and expiry. Because the digest matches, SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow succeeds and the swap executes without the signer's intention. ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. Kyber deploys UniswapV4KEMHook on Ethereum mainnet with a specific PoolKey
2. Same hook (or same PoolKey configuration) is deployed on Arbitrum using CREATE3 salt mining to get matching address
3. User requests a quote on Ethereum, quoteSigner signs: keccak256(abi.encode(sender, key, zeroForOne, maxAmountIn, maxExchangeRate, exchangeRateDenom, nonce, expiryTime))
4. User broadcasts swap transaction on Ethereum mainnet
5. Attacker observes the transaction in Ethereum mempool, extracts signature and hookData
6. Attacker submits identical calldata on Arbitrum before expiryTime
7. On Arbitrum: sender (router) matches, key matches (same pool configuration), all other parameters match
8. SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow(quoteSigner, digest, signature) returns true

ground_truth.description: Both hooks accept swaps when SignatureChecker validates keccak256(abi.encode(sender, key, ..., nonce, expiryTime)). The sender field is the router contract that called the pool manager. That restricts execution to Kyber's router, but not to any particular user. Because the router is public, anyone can forward the calldata and signature. If Alice broadcasts a signed swap, an MEV bot can copy the calldata, submit it first and the hook sees the same router address and quote terms: the attacker's swap succeeds, consuming the nonce. Alice's transaction then reverts at _useUnorderedNonce because the nonce is already marked as used. The attacker, this way, can invalidate the quote with a dust swap. Designers intended router-level exclusivity, yet end users receive no front-running protection, exposing every quote to mempool sniping.

2. Kyber quoteSigner signs the quote with parameters: sender=router, maxAmountIn=100e18, maxExchangeRate, nonce=12345, expiryTime=now+60s
3. Alice constructs swap transaction and broadcasts to mempool
4. MEV bot observes Alice's pending transaction, extracts hookData containing signature

Inside V2Locker.unlock(), the contract sets lockedUntil = 0 (via delete lockedUntil) before transferring the LP tokens to the recipient. During the LP token transfer, the underlying pool credits all accumulated fees to the locker contract. Once the LP tokens are transferred out, the locker can no longer call claimFees() because it is no longer locked (lockedUntil == 0), leaving those fees permanently stranded on the contract. A user who forgets to call claimFees() before unlocking will lose the entire fee balance earned up to that moment.

ground_truth.description: The isProposalOpen() function returns true if a proposal is open for voting. It returns false if it's too late OR too early for voting. But in _withdrawActiveVotingPower() at line 225, it was being used as an 'isProposalStillOpen()' function, forgetting that it will also be false when the proposal hasn't started yet. This means proposals with future start dates get incorrectly removed from knownProposalIds tracking.
ground_truth.root_cause: The isProposalOpen() function returns true if a proposal is open for voting. It returns false if it's too late OR too early for voting. But in _withdrawActiveVotingPower() at line 225, it was being used as an 'isProposalStillOpen()' function, forgetting that it will also be false when the proposal hasn't started yet. This means proposals with future start dates get incorrectly removed from knownProposalIds tracking.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. A proposal is created with a future start date (e.g., starts in 1 week).
2. User calls unlock() before the proposal starts.
3. _withdrawActiveVotingPower() is called at line 135.
4. Line 225: plugin.isProposalOpen(_proposalId) returns false (proposal hasn't started).
5. Line 226: knownProposalIds.remove(_proposalId) - proposal removed from tracking.
6. Proposal starts a week later, user votes.
7. User calls unlock() again - vote isn't cleared because proposal isn't tracked.
8. User withdraws tokens while still having active votes.
ground_truth.fix_description: Create and use an isProposalEnded() function specifically for this use case. It should return true only if the proposal has actually ended (endDate passed or executed), not just because it hasn't started.

ground_truth.description: Governance can configure `DynamicSwapFeeModule` with fees up to 50%, but `CLFactory.getSwapFee` discards any value above 100_000 ppm (10%) and falls back to the tick-spacing default (often 500 ppm = 0.05%) without reverting or logging. Operators see the module reporting 20%, yet users continue paying the tiny default fee. The silent fallback misleads governance into believing higher fees are active. Impact - Governance believes a protective high fee is set (e.g., during launch anti-MEV), but the effective fee drops back to the default (e.g., 0.05%). - Traders are charged far less than intended, defeating protective or revenue objectives. - The misconfiguration has no on-chain signal, so the mistake can persist unnoticed. Root Cause - getSwapFee checks fee <= 100_000 ; larger values are ignored and the function returns tickSpacingToFee . - The module itself allows feeCap up to 500_000 (50%), so governance can set a value the factory immediately discards in favor of the default.

PoC source ( `cl/test/PoC_DynamicFee_ClampToDefault.t.sol` ): // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT pragma solidity 0.7.6; pragma abicoder v2; import "forge-std/Test.sol"; import {C4PoCTestbed} from "./C4PoCTestbed.t.sol"; import {DynamicSwapFeeModule} from "contracts/core/fees/DynamicSwapFeeModule.sol"; contract PoC_DynamicFee_ClampToDefault is C4PoCTestbed { address internal pool; function setUp() public override { super.setUp(); pool = poolFactory.createPool(USDC, DAI, 100, uint160(2 ** 96)); require(pool != address(0), "pool not created"); } function testFactoryClampsFeeAboveTenPercent() public { address manager = poolFactory.swapFeeManager(); vm.prank(manager); swapFeeModule.setFeeCap(pool, 500_000); // raise module cap to 50% vm.prank(manager); swapFeeModule.setScalingFactor(pool, 1); // ensure positive TWAP delta doesn't zero fee uint24 highFee = 200_000; // 20% vm.prank(manager); swapFeeModule.setCustomFee(pool, highFee); uint24 moduleFee = swapFeeModule.getFee(pool); assertEq(uint256(moduleFee), uint256(highFee), "module reports configured fee"); uint24 factoryFee = poolFactory.getSwapFee(pool); assertEq(uint256(factoryFee), 500, "factory silently clamps to tick-spacing default"); } }

vulnerabilities.explanation: createProposal accepts arbitrary Action[] without validating targets. When proposal.targetConfig.operation == DelegateCall, actions with .to == address(lockManager) execute in the plugin's context, allowing direct calls to lockManager.proposalEnded().

Calls createProposal with _actions[0] = {to: lockManager, data: proposalEnded(proposalId)} and targetConfig set to DelegateCall. 3. Proposal is stored and lockManager.proposalCreated is called. 4. vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: In createProposal, before the loop: for (uint256 i; i < _actions.length; ++i) { if (_actions[i].to == address(this) || _actions[i].to == address(lockManager)) revert InvalidTarget(); }

ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. A 'normal' proposal_1 is created ending in 1 year.
2. Alice locks 100 tokens, votes NO on proposal_1.
3. Attacker creates proposal_2 with action: LockManager.proposalEnded(proposal_1_id).
4. proposal_2 passes and executes.
5. proposalEnded(proposal_1) is called via delegatecall from the plugin.
6. proposal_1 is removed from knownProposalIds.
7. Alice calls unlock() - her NO vote is not cleared because proposal_1 isn't tracked.
8. Alice withdraws tokens while her vote is still active on proposal_1.

ground_truth.fix_description: Remove the realizedPremium != 0 guard. Derive commission directly from premium when shortAmount == 0 && longAmount == 0.

ground_truth.fix_description: Include validUntil and validAfter in the signed hash computation before applying the EIP-191 prefix. Conditionally incorporate metadata values when a 77-byte signature is present.

ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. Configurator sets up phantom token A tracking output token USDC via setTokenAllowedStatusBatch()
2. phantomTokenToOutputToken[phantomA] = USDC
3. User makes a redemption request for output token USDT (different from USDC)
4. pendingRedemptions records the request with tokenOut = USDT
5. User calls withdrawPhantomToken(phantomA, amount)

7. Function calls _withdraw(amount) which executes Gateway.withdraw()

2. erc20Token.transferFrom() returns false but doesn't revert.

ground_truth.attack_scenario: function test_submissionValidity() external { // first depositor attack address alice = makeAddr("alice"); address bob = makeAddr("bob"); vm.startPrank(address(minter)); hybr.mint(alice, 2000e18); hybr.mint(bob, 100e18); vm.stopPrank(); vm.startPrank(alice); hybr.approve(address(gHybr), type(uint).max); gHybr.deposit(2, alice); hybr.transfer(address(gHybr), 1000e18); // alice transfers 1000 HYBR to gHYBR gHybr.receivePenaltyReward(1000e18); // alice donates 1000 through the receivePenaltyReward function vm.stopPrank(); // bob deposits vm.startPrank(bob); hybr.approve(address(gHybr), 100e18); gHybr.deposit(100e18, bob); vm.stopPrank(); console.log("alice's shares: ", gHybr.balanceOf(alice)); console.log("bob's shares: ", gHybr.balanceOf(bob)); console.log("gHYBR total assets: ", gHybr.totalAssets()); } Run this test and see the result: - Alice’s shares: 2 - Bob’s shares: 0 - gHYBR total assets: 1100000000000000000002 Alice captures all of Bob’s deposits.

vulnerabilities.explanation: When signatureFlag & 0x40 == 0 (checkpointer disabled) and signature type is chained (0x01), recover skips the entire checkpointer block leaving snapshot unset (bytes32(0)). recoverChained then calls recover with _ignoreCheckpointer=true and passes the zeroed snapshot forward; final validation at recoverChained:140 and recover:140 succeeds because snapshot.imageHash remains zero, bypassing any enforced checkpointer.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: Attacker (evicted signer) crafts a chained signature with bit 6 unset; calls recoverChained on a payload valid under a stale config; checkpointer validation is never executed so the signature is accepted and state-changing operations (e.g. config update) succeed without the required checkpoint proof.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: In recover, before the chained branch: if ((signatureFlag & 0x01 == 0x01) && (signatureFlag & 0x40 == 0)) revert MissingCheckpointer();

vulnerabilities.explanation: storeOraclePack places _currentResiduals (uint96) at bits 12-107 via <<12, while referenceTick occupies bits 96-117 and EMAs start at 120. This causes overlap and truncation into higher fields. The low 12 bits receive only the new residual, but the shift misaligns the entire 96-bit residual block against the documented layout (residuals must occupy 0-95).
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Call insertObservation with a newTick that does not trigger rebase. 2. storeOraclePack overwrites bits 96-107 of referenceTick/lockMode with residual data. 3. Subsequent calls to referenceTick(), residualTick(), getMedianTick(), or getEMAs() return corrupted values. 4. Any protocol using the resulting medianTick/EMAs for liquidations, settlements or TWAP pricing settles at attacker-controlled prices.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Change the residual placement to uint256(_currentResiduals) (no <<12) and insert the new residual by shifting the uint96 right by 12 bits and OR-ing the new 12-bit value into the LSB before storing, ensuring residuals stay in bits 0-95.

vulnerabilities.explanation: The function unconditionally calls safePermit() with user-supplied v,r,s before _unstakeRequest. vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Wrap the permit call in try-catch; if permit fails but allowance[msg.sender][this] >= methAmount, proceed with _unstakeRequest.

ground_truth.description: An attacker can read the v, r, s from the mempool and call mETH.permit() first, consuming the user's signature and updating the nonce. The subsequent user transaction Staking.unstakeRequestWithPermit() then reverts on the permit() call due to an invalidated signature/nonce, preventing the unstake flow from executing, even though allowance is already set.

The subsequent user transaction Staking.unstakeRequestWithPermit() then reverts on the permit() call due to an invalidated signature/nonce, preventing the unstake flow from executing, even though allowance is already set.
ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. User submits unstakeRequestWithPermit() transaction with signature (v, r, s) to the mempool
2. Attacker monitors mempool and extracts the permit signature parameters
3. Attacker front-runs with a direct call to mETH.permit() using the extracted (v, r, s)
4. The permit succeeds, consuming the user's nonce and setting the allowance
5. User's original unstakeRequestWithPermit() transaction is mined
6. The SafeERC20Upgradeable.safePermit() call inside unstakeRequestWithPermit() reverts because the nonce is already used
7. User's unstake request fails even though the allowance was set
ground_truth.fix_description: Wrap the permit() invocation in a try-catch clause and proceed with the unstake if allowance is already sufficient, avoiding a hard revert when signatures are pre-consumed.

vulnerabilities.explanation: Nonce is consumed via _consumeNonce before _execute. When any call uses BEHAVIOR_REVERT_ON_ERROR and fails, Reverted() causes the entire transaction to revert, rolling back the nonce. The original _signature (validated on the full decoded payload) remains usable. Per-call error handling and individual call processing enable replay of the same signature for full or partial execution sequences.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. Submit payload with calls [A,B,C] and valid signature S where B has BEHAVIOR_REVERT_ON_ERROR. 2. Frontrunner or attacker triggers execution; B fails and reverts. 3. Nonce is rolled back. 4. Attacker immediately replays identical (or subset) payload + S to execute A and/or C again, bypassing intended single-use semantics.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Consume nonce only after successful execution of the entire payload, or bind signature to a hash that includes a unique nonce committed before any execution and never rolled back on inner reverts. Validate signatures against the complete payload hash only.

ground_truth.description: When a session call with BEHAVIOR_REVERT_ON_ERROR fails, the transaction reverts but nonce is not consumed. The signature remains valid and can be replayed for partial calls. Session signatures are validated per-call using individual call hashes, enabling partial replay. Frontrunners can execute subsets of calls to grief or cause financial loss.
ground_truth.root_cause: When a session call with BEHAVIOR_REVERT_ON_ERROR fails, the transaction reverts but nonce is not consumed. The signature remains valid and can be replayed for partial calls. Session signatures are validated per-call using individual call hashes, enabling partial replay. Frontrunners can execute subsets of calls to grief or cause financial loss.
ground_truth.attack_scenario: Original payload: Calls [A, B, C] with signatures [SigA, SigB, SigC]. Execution: [A succeed, B succeed, C revert]. Result: Revert, nonce unused. ground_truth.fix_description: Bind session call signatures to the complete payload hash to prevent partial signature replay.

vulnerabilities.explanation: In _vote(), _poolWeight = _weights[i] * _weight / _totalVoteWeight is computed and then require(_poolWeight != 0, 'ZV') is enforced. An attacker can split votes such that one pool receives a 1-wei allocation. After veNFT decay, this 1-wei scaled by the new (smaller) _weight rounds to zero.

Any poke() attempt (via owner or ve deposit) hits require(_poolWeight != 0) on pool B and reverts. 4. Pool A retains the original (now inflated) weight, distorting bribe distribution.

ground_truth.description: Before describing the vulnerability, we should know that in ve3.3 systems, `poke` is important to make anyone reflect the decaying vote weight to prevent users from being inactive on votes to have their full weight votes on a pool. In `VoterV3` users choose what pools they want to vote for and the contract retrieves their `ve` weight upon doing so: uint256 _weight = IVotingEscrow(_ve).balanceOfNFT(_tokenId); And upon voting for a pool, that weight affects the claimable share distribution of that pool compared to other pools. Since now we know the importance of the voting weight, and since ve NFT weight decay with time, there is a poke function to update the voting weight made on a pool previously to the decayed weight of that NFT. The `poke()` function is guarded to be called by the owner or through the `ve` contract which can have anyone depositing for a user or increasing his locked value even by `1wei` to poke him to reflect his new decayed weight on the voted pools. An attacker can do the following: 1. vote his full weight - 1wei on a dedicated pool 2. vote 1 wei on another pool 3. time passes with inactivity from his side - his ve decay but is not reflected on voted pools 4. users try to poke() him through known functions of the ve contract 5. poke() function reverts here File: VoterV3.sol 208: uint256 _poolWeight = _weights[i] * _weight / _totalVoteWeight; 209:  210: require(votes[_tokenId][_pool] == 0, "ZV"); 211: require(_poolWeight != 0, "ZV"); Since the `1wei` vote multiplied by the decayed weight divided by totalVoteWeight rounds down to 0, hence this user becomes unpokable. Impact: The voted for pool will have inflated rewards distributed to him compared to other pools that have pokable users. Thinking of this attack at scale, the user will have advantage of having full voting weight if he votes immediately like having permanent lock weight without actually locking his balance permanently. Preventing anyone from preserving this invariant `A single veNFT’s total vote allocation ≤ its available voting power.` on his vote balance too.

ground_truth.description: StakingBase._claim() and _withdraw() violate CEI by calling the virtual _transfer() function before updating persistent balance state. The virtual function can invoke token callbacks or receiver fallbacks, enabling reentrancy.

ground_truth.attack_scenario: Attacker calls withdraw which triggers _transfer callback. During callback, attacker reenters to claim or withdraw again. State not yet updated from first call, so full balance is available for second extraction.
ground_truth.fix_description: Apply reentrancy guards to claim/withdraw/create. Reorder external interactions to follow CEI strictly.

vulnerabilities.explanation: Returns erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this)) without capping to actual balance. Unlimited approvals (type(uint256).max) cause subsequent transfer to request impossible amount.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario: 1. User calls approve(lockManager, type(uint256).max). 2. User calls lock(). 3. _incomingTokenBalance returns max uint. 4. _doLockTransfer reverts on transferFrom due to insufficient balance.
vulnerabilities.suggested_fix: Return min(allowance, balanceOf(msg.sender)) in _incomingTokenBalance.

ground_truth.description: The lock() function intends to lock the user's entire approved balance, but this will fail for the most common case: Most users give contracts they interact with an unlimited allowance by setting it to type(uint256).max. The _incomingTokenBalance() function at line 32 returns just 'erc20Token.allowance(msg.sender, address(this))' which would be type(uint256).max for unlimited approvals. The lock() function then attempts to transfer this impossible amount.

ground_truth.attack_scenario:
1. User approves LockManager with unlimited allowance: approve(lockManager, type(uint256).max).
2. User calls lock() without specifying an amount.
3. _incomingTokenBalance() returns type(uint256).max.
4. _doLockTransfer attempts to transfer type(uint256).max tokens.
5. Transaction reverts because user doesn't have that many tokens.
6. User cannot use the standard lock() function.
ground_truth.fix_description: Have _incomingTokenBalance() return either the actual balance or the allowance depending on whichever is smallest: 'return (allowance >= balance) ? balance : allowance;'
